Extending Laptop Price Analysis Using Tidyverse

DATA 607 - Tidyverse EXTEND Assignment

Author

Patricio Romero

Published

November 15, 2026

1 Introduction

This project extends Andre Thomson’s original vignette, Laptop Prices with Tidyverse.

The original project used Tidyverse functions to clean laptop data, compare prices by category, and identify laptops that meet specific RAM and storage requirements.

This extension explores how laptop prices vary by brand and hardware specifications. Additional Tidyverse functions, data transformations, and visualizations are used to better understand these relationships.

2 Research Questions

  1. How do laptop prices vary across brands?

  2. How does RAM capacity relate to laptop prices?

  3. How does storage capacity relate to laptop prices?

  4. How does CPU core count relate to laptop prices?

  5. Which combinations of RAM and storage are associated with higher laptop prices?

3 Data Source

This extension uses the same dataset as the original vignette created by Andre Thomson.

  • Dataset: Laptops Cleaned Dataset
  • Source: Kaggle
  • File: Andre_Thomson_laptops.csv
  • Observations: 992
  • Variables: 27
  • Currency: Indian Rupees (INR)

Using the same dataset allows this extension to build on the original analysis while exploring additional relationships.

4 Load Packages

The Tidyverse package is used to import, clean, transform, and visualize the data. The knitr package is used to display tables.

Show code 
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(scales)

5 Data Import

The original dataset is imported using the read_csv() function from the readr package.

The original data remains unchanged. The following tables show the dataset size and a preview of the main variables used in this extension.

)

Before starting the analysis, I check the quality of the dataset to identify missing values and duplicate records.

6.1 Dataset Quality Overview

Show code 
# Check the quality of the original dataset
data_quality <- tibble(
  Description = c(
    "Total Laptop Records",
    "Total Variables",
    "Total Data Values",
    "Missing Values",
    "Duplicate Records"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(laptops_raw),
    ncol(laptops_raw),
    nrow(laptops_raw) * ncol(laptops_raw),

6.2 Missing Values Analysis

The following table shows the variables with missing values and the percentage of missing data. Variable names are formatted to make the table easier to read.

Show code 
# Identify missing values by variable
missing_summary <- laptops_raw |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  ) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0) |>
  mutate(
    missing_percentage = round(
      missing_values / nrow(laptops_raw) * 100, 2
    ),

    # Standardize variable names for presentation
    variable = recode(
      variable,
      "cpu_lp_e_cores" = "CPU Low-Power E-Cores",
      "gpu_vram_gb" = "GPU VRAM (GB)",
      "cpu_e_cores" = "CPU Efficiency Cores",
      "cpu_p_cores" = "CPU Performance Cores",
      "cpu_suffix" = "CPU Suffix",
      "gpu_brand" = "GPU Brand",
      "gpu_series" = "GPU Series",
      "gpu_model" = "GPU Model",
      "gpu_type" = "GPU Type"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_values))

knitr::kable(
  missing_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Variable",
    "Missing Values",
    "Missing Percentage (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Missing Values by Variable",
  row.names = FALSE,
  digits = 2
)

6.3 Interpretation

The dataset contains 992 laptop records and 27 variables. There are 2,289 missing values and no duplicate records.

Most missing values are related to CPU and GPU details. However, the main variables selected for this extension have no missing values.

For this reason, I can continue the analysis without removing laptop records.

6.4 Visualizing Missing Values

This chart helps identify the variables with the highest percentage of missing data.

Show code 
ggplot(
  missing_summary,
  aes(
    x = reorder(variable, missing_percentage),
    y = missing_percentage
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "steelblue",
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(missing_percentage, "%")),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100)

  labs(

    subtitle = "Laptop Prices Dataset",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Missing Percentage (%)",
    caption = "Source: Andre Thomson's Laptop Dataset"

    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),

7 Data Cleaning and Transformation

In this section, I use Tidyverse functions to prepare the data for further analysis.

The original dataset remains unchanged.

7.1 Select Variables and Standardize Names

The select() function keeps the variables needed for this analysis. The mutate() function is used to standardize laptop brand names.

Show code 
# Select the main variables
laptops_clean <- laptops_raw |>
  select(
    brand,
    model,
    device_category,
    price,
    ram_gb,
    storage_gb,
    cpu_core_count
  ) |>
  mutate(
    brand = str_to_title(brand),
    brand = recode(
      brand,
      "Hp" = "HP",
      "Asus" = "ASUS",
      "Msi" = "MSI"
    )
  )

# Display the selected variables
knitr::kable(
  head(laptops_clean, 10),
  col.names = c(
    "Brand",
    "Laptop Model",
    "Device Category",
    "Price (INR)",
    "RAM (GB)",
    "Storage (GB)",
    "CPU Cores"
  ),
  caption = "Selected Laptop Variables",
  row.names = FALSE,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)

7.2 Currency Conversion (INR to USD)

The original laptop prices are in Indian Rupees (INR). I use the mutate() function to create a new variable with prices in US Dollars (USD).

The conversion uses the 2025 average exchange rate of 87.1468 INR per USD.

Show code 
# Set the 2025 average exchange rate
exchange_rate <- 87.1468

# Convert laptop prices to US Dollars
laptops_clean <- laptops_clean |>
  mutate(
    price_usd = price / exchange_rate
  ) |>
  relocate(price_usd, .after = price)

# Display the converted prices
laptops_clean |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(
    price = scales::comma(price),
    price_usd = scales::dollar(price_usd, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Brand",
      "Laptop Model",
      "Device Category",
      "Price (INR)",
      "Price (USD)",
      "RAM (GB)",
      "Storage (GB)",
      "CPU Cores"
    ),
    caption = "Laptop Prices in INR and USD",
    row.names = FALSE
  )
Laptop Prices in INR and USD

7.3 Interpretation

I used select() to keep the main variables and mutate() to standardize brand names and convert prices to US Dollars.

I also used relocate() to place both price variables next to each other.

This transformation makes the prices easier to understand and compare. The USD values are estimates of the original prices in India.

8 Laptop Price Analysis by Brand

In this section, I compare laptop prices across different brands.

The group_by() and summarise() functions are used to calculate the number of laptops and their average, median, minimum, and maximum prices.

8.1 Price Summary by Brand

Show code 
# Calculate price statistics by brand
brand_summary <- laptops_clean |>
  group_by(brand) |>
  summarise(
    total_laptops = n(),
    average_price = mean(price_usd),
    median_price = median(price_usd),
    minimum_price = min(price_usd),
    maximum_price = max(price_usd),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_price))

# Display the price summary
brand_summary |>
  mutate(
    across(
      ends_with("_price"),
      ~ scales::dollar(.x, accuracy = 0.01)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Brand",
      "Total Laptops",
      "Average Price (USD)",
      "Median Price (USD)",
      "Minimum Price (USD)",
      "Maximum Price (USD)"
    ),
    caption = "Laptop Price Summary by Brand",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

8.2 Top 10 Most Common Laptop Brands

The slice_max() function selects the ten brands with the highest number of laptop records.

Show code 
# Select the ten most common brands
top_brands <- brand_summary |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = total_laptops,
    n = 10,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_laptops))

# Display the most common brands
top_brands |>
  select(
    brand,
    total_laptops,
    average_price,
    median_price
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      ends_with("_price"),
      ~ scales::dollar(.x, accuracy = 0.01)
    )
  ) |>

      "Brand",
      "Total Laptops",
      "Average Price (USD)",

8.3 Median Laptop Price by Brand

The median price is used because it is less affected by very high or very low prices.

The fct_reorder() function organizes the brands based on their median prices.

Show code 
ggplot(
  top_brands,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(brand, median_price),
    y = median_price,
    fill = brand
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.7,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = scales::dollar(
        median_price,
        accuracy = 1
      )
    ),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    title = "Median Laptop Price by Brand",
    subtitle = "Comparison of the Top 10 Most Common Brands",
    x = "Laptop Brand",
    y = "Median Price (USD)",
    caption = "Source: Andre Thomson's Laptop Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

9 RAM and Laptop Price Analysis

In this section, I explore how laptop prices vary by RAM capacity.

I use the group_by() and summarise() functions to compare laptop prices across different RAM sizes.

9.1 Price Summary by RAM Capacity

Show code 
# Calculate price statistics by RAM capacity
ram_summary <- laptops_clean |>
  group_by(ram_gb) |>
  summarise(
    total_laptops = n(),
    average_price = mean(price_usd),
    median_price = median(price_usd),
    minimum_price = min(price_usd),
    maximum_price = max(price_usd),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(ram_gb)

# Display the RAM price summary
ram_summary |>
  mutate(
    ram_gb = paste(ram_gb, "GB"),
    across(
      ends_with("_price"),
      ~ scales::dollar(.x, accuracy = 0.01)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "RAM Capacity",
      "Total Laptops",
      "Average Price (USD)",
      "Median Price (USD)",
      "Minimum Price (USD)",
      "Maximum Price (USD)"
    ),
    caption = "Laptop Price Summary by RAM Capacity",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

9.2 Laptop Price Distribution by RAM

The geom_boxplot() function shows the distribution of laptop prices for each RAM capacity.

This chart helps compare median prices, price variation, and unusually high or low prices.

Show code 
ggplot(
  laptops_clean,
  aes(
    x = factor(ram_gb),
    y = price_usd,
    fill = factor(ram_gb)
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.85,
    outlier.alpha = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(
    palette = "Paired"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_dollar()
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = function(x) paste(x, "GB")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Laptop Price Distribution by RAM Capacity",
    subtitle = "Comparison of Laptop Prices in USD",
    x = "RAM Capacity",
    y = "Laptop Price (USD)",
    caption = "Source: Andre Thomson's Laptop Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

10 Storage and Laptop Price Analysis

In this section, I explore how laptop prices vary by storage capacity.

I use the case_when() function to display storage capacity in GB or TB, making the results easier to understand.

10.1 Price Summary by Storage Capacity

Show code 
# Create readable storage capacity labels
laptops_clean <- laptops_clean |>
  mutate(
    storage_label = case_when(
      storage_gb >= 1024 ~ paste(storage_gb / 1024, "TB"),
      TRUE ~ paste(storage_gb, "GB")
    )
  )

# Calculate price statistics by storage capacity
storage_summary <- laptops_clean |>
  group_by(storage_gb, storage_label) |>
  summarise(
    total_laptops = n(),
    average_price = mean(price_usd),
    median_price = median(price_usd),
    minimum_price = min(price_usd),
    maximum_price = max(price_usd),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(storage_gb)

# Display the storage price summary
storage_summary |>
  select(-storage_gb) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      ends_with("_price"),
      ~ scales::dollar(.x, accuracy = 0.01)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Storage Capacity",
      "Total Laptops",
      "Average Price (USD)",
      "Median Price (USD)",
      "Minimum Price (USD)",
      "Maximum Price (USD)"
    ),
    caption = "Laptop Price Summary by Storage Capacity",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

    caption = "Source: Andre Thomson's Laptop Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

11 CPU Core Count and Laptop Price Analysis

In this section, I explore the relationship between the number of CPU cores and laptop prices.

The purpose is to identify whether laptops with more CPU cores tend to have higher prices.

11.2 CPU Core Count vs. Laptop Price

The geom_point() function displays individual laptop prices, while geom_smooth() adds a trend line.

Different colors represent different laptop categories.

Show code 
ggplot(
  laptops_clean,
  aes(
    x = cpu_core_count,
    y = price_usd
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = device_category),
    size = 2.6,
    alpha = 0.55,
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.35,
      height = 0,
      seed = 123
    )
  ) +

  # Add the overall trend line
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    color = "#263238",
    fill = "#90A4AE",
    linewidth = 1.3,
    linetype = "dashed",
    se = TRUE
  ) +

  # Assign a color to each laptop category
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Business" = "#0072B2",
      "Convertible" = "#E69F00",
      "Gaming" = "#D55E00",
      "General" = "#009E73",
      "Thin & Light" = "#CC79A7"
    )
  ) +

  # Display actual CPU core counts
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(laptops_clean$cpu_core_count))
  ) +

  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    breaks = scales::breaks_width(1000)
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "CPU Core Count vs. Laptop Price",
    subtitle = "Price Distribution and Overall Trend by Laptop Category",
    x = "Number of CPU Cores",
    y = "Laptop Price (USD)",
    color = "Device Category",
    caption = "Source: Andre Thomson's Laptop Dataset"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +

  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 19
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      color = "gray40",
      size = 10
    )
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)
  )

11.3 Interpretation

The chart shows a positive relationship between CPU core count and laptop prices.

Laptops with more CPU cores generally have higher prices. Gaming laptops are also among the most expensive models.

However, laptops with the same number of CPU cores can have different prices. This suggests that other hardware specifications may also affect laptop prices.

12 Combined RAM and Storage Analysis

In this section, I analyze RAM and storage capacity together to compare laptop prices.

The purpose is to identify which hardware combinations are associated with higher or lower prices.

    median_price = median(price_usd),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>

12.2 RAM and Storage Price Heatmap

The geom_tile() function creates a heatmap to compare median prices across different combinations of RAM and storage.

Darker colors represent higher median prices. Each cell also shows the median price and the number of laptop records.

Show code 
ggplot(
  ram_storage_summary,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(storage_label, storage_gb),
    y = factor(ram_gb),
    fill = median_price
  )
) +

  # Create the heatmap
  geom_tile(
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +

  # Display median prices and record counts
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = paste0(
        scales::dollar(median_price, accuracy = 1),
        "\n(n = ", total_laptops, ")"
      ),
      color = median_price > 2000
    ),
    size = 3.2,
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 0.95
  ) +

  # Set the price color scale
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#E3F2FD",
    high = "#0D477D",
    labels = scales::label_dollar()
  ) +

  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "black", "TRUE" = "white"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +

  scale_y_discrete(
    labels = function(x) paste(x, "GB")
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "Median Laptop Price by RAM and Storage",
    subtitle = "Combined Hardware Specifications",
    x = "Storage Capacity",
    y = "RAM Capacity",
    fill = "Median Price (USD)",
    caption = "Source: Andre Thomson's Laptop Dataset"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +

  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 19
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(2, "cm")
  )

13 Results and Discussion

This extension uses additional Tidyverse functions to explore laptop prices based on brand, RAM, storage capacity, and CPU core count.

13.2 Tidyverse Functions Used in This Extension

The following table summarizes the main functions used to extend the original vignette.

Tidyverse Functions Used in the Extension
Function Package Purpose
mutate() dplyr Convert prices from INR to USD.
relocate() dplyr Organize price columns.
case_when() dplyr Create GB and TB storage labels.
slice_max() dplyr Identify the most common brands.
fct_reorder() forcats Organize chart categories.
geom_boxplot() ggplot2 Compare price distributions.
geom_smooth() ggplot2 Show the overall price trend.
geom_tile() ggplot2 Compare RAM and storage together.

13.3 Discussion

The original vignette focused on laptop categories and basic hardware requirements.

This extension provides a more detailed analysis of laptop prices by brand, RAM, storage capacity, and CPU core count.

The conversion from INR to USD makes the prices easier to understand.

The different tables and visualizations help compare hardware specifications and identify price patterns.

The CPU analysis shows that laptops with more CPU cores generally have higher prices. However, price differences may also depend on other specifications and device categories.

13.4 Limitations

This analysis has some limitations:

  • The dataset represents the laptop market in India.
  • Prices in USD are estimated using an average exchange rate.
  • Some hardware combinations have fewer laptop records.
  • Other factors, such as GPU performance and processor generation, may also be related to laptop prices.
  • The results show relationships between variables but do not prove causation.

14 Conclusion

In this project, I extended Andre Thomson’s original vignette using additional Tidyverse functions.

I converted laptop prices from INR to USD and explored the relationship between prices and different hardware specifications.

I also created additional tables, bar charts, boxplots, a scatter plot, and a heatmap.

This assignment helped me better understand how Tidyverse functions work together to clean, transform, summarize, and visualize real-world data.

It also helped me practice collaboration with GitHub by building on another student’s work.

15 AI Use

ChatGPT was used to help understand the assignment requirements, review the original vignette, organize the extension, improve the English writing, and provide guidance on R code and Tidyverse functions.

I reviewed the code, tables, and visualizations during the development of this extension.
